Romans 1.audience: Roman believers who knew Paul only by reputation, and whose own faith was already spoken of across the empire (Romans 1:8), would have read this long, careful introduction as an apostle earning a hearing before he arrived.

culture.title: Paul's letter opening
culture.text: Greek letters opened with the sender, the recipients, and a greeting. Paul's opening here is the longest in his letters.

culture.title: Greeks and Barbarians
culture.text: Greeks called anyone who did not speak Greek a ‘barbarian,’ after the sound of foreign speech.

culture.title: Images of animals
culture.text: Egyptian religion worshiped gods in the form of birds, beasts, and serpents. Greek and Roman temples held images of gods in human form.

Romans 2.audience: Paul writes as if answering a questioner, a style called diatribe, addressing someone who judges others and one who calls himself a Jew (Romans 2:1, 17).

culture.title: The diatribe
culture.text: Greek teachers such as the Stoic Epictetus taught by addressing an imaginary opponent, "O man," and answering objections.

culture.title: Robbing temples
culture.text: Temples stored treasure and offerings. Deuteronomy 7:25 forbade Israel from taking the silver and gold of idols.

culture.title: Circumcision
culture.text: Circumcision marked Jewish males as members of the covenant (Genesis 17:10–14). Greeks and Romans often mocked it.

Romans 3.audience: Jewish and Gentile hearers in Rome who knew the Psalms and Isaiah would have recognized each quoted line, and felt the weight of hearing them strung together as a single verdict on everyone.

culture.title: The oracles of God
culture.text: Israel had been entrusted with the Scriptures, which were read in synagogues across the empire.

culture.title: A chain of Scripture
culture.text: Linking passages from several books was a common Jewish teaching method. Here Paul draws on Psalms 14, 5, 140, 10, and 36 and Isaiah 59.

culture.title: Propitiation
culture.text: The Greek word is also used in the Greek Old Testament for the mercy seat, the lid of the ark sprinkled with blood on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14–15).

Romans 4.audience: Paul uses Abraham and David as examples from Scripture, quoting Genesis 15:6 and Psalm 32:1–2.

culture.title: Counted for righteousness
culture.text: The word "counted" (also "reckoned" and "imputed") was an accounting term for crediting an amount to someone's account.

culture.title: Abraham before circumcision
culture.text: In Genesis, Abraham is counted righteous in chapter 15; he is circumcised in chapter 17.

culture.title: About an hundred years old
culture.text: Abraham was ninety-nine when circumcised and a hundred when Isaac was born; Sarah was ninety (Genesis 17:17; 21:5).

Romans 5.audience: Paul compares Adam and Christ, tracing sin and death from Adam (Genesis 3) to the law of Moses.

culture.title: Dying for a good man
culture.text: Greek and Roman stories honored those who died for friends or country.

culture.title: Access
culture.text: The Greek word could describe being brought into the presence of a ruler.

culture.title: From Adam to Moses
culture.text: Paul refers to the generations of Genesis 5–11 who lived before the law was given at Sinai.

Romans 6.audience: Paul answers the question "Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?" (Romans 6:1) using pictures of baptism and slavery.

culture.title: Baptism by immersion
culture.text: Early Christian baptism was usually done by going down into water. Paul describes it as being "buried with him by baptism."

culture.title: Slavery in Rome
culture.text: Slaves made up a large part of Rome's population. A slave owed full obedience to his master, and could be freed or sold to a new owner.

culture.title: Wages
culture.text: The word for wages was used for a soldier's pay or rations.

Romans 7.audience: Believers who knew the law of Moses would have followed the marriage illustration easily, since the rule that a husband's death frees his wife from her obligation was familiar in Jewish and Roman households alike.

culture.title: Bound by the law while the husband lives
culture.text: Under the law of Moses a married woman was bound to her husband while he lived and free to remarry after his death (compare 1 Corinthians 7:39).

culture.title: Thou shalt not covet
culture.text: Paul quotes the tenth commandment (Exodus 20:17).

Romans 8.audience: Believers living under a government that could turn on them would have heard the closing list of things that cannot separate them from God's love as an answer to fears they actually carried.

culture.title: Adoption
culture.text: In Roman adoption a son came under his new father's authority and became his full legal heir, even if adopted as an adult.

culture.title: Abba
culture.text: Paul keeps the Aramaic word for father, as Jesus used it in prayer (Mark 14:36).

culture.title: Sheep for the slaughter
culture.text: Paul quotes Psalm 44:22, a lament of Israel suffering though faithful to God.

Romans 9.audience: Jewish believers in Rome would have recognized a fellow Israelite grieving for his own people, while Gentile believers would have been reminded that the promises they now shared were first Israel's.

culture.title: Israel's privileges
culture.text: Paul lists the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the service of God, the promises, and the fathers.

culture.title: Jacob and Esau
culture.text: Paul cites Genesis 25:23 and Malachi 1:2–3 about the twins born to Rebecca.

culture.title: The potter and the clay
culture.text: Potters shaped vessels for honored and common use from the same lump of clay. The prophets used the image (Isaiah 29:16; 45:9; Jeremiah 18:1–6).

Romans 10.audience: Hearers would have taken from the chain of questions about calling, believing, hearing, preaching, and sending that the message depends on messengers, including the letter they were then listening to.

culture.title: The end of the law
culture.text: The Greek word telos can mean ‘end,’ ‘goal,’ or ‘completion.’

culture.title: Confessing with the mouth
culture.text: ‘Lord’ (kyrios) was used in the Greek Old Testament for God's name and was also a title claimed for the emperor.

culture.title: Beautiful feet
culture.text: Messengers ran on foot to bring news. Paul quotes Isaiah 52:7.

Romans 11.audience: Paul addresses the Gentile believers directly: "I speak to you Gentiles" (Romans 11:13).

culture.title: Seven thousand
culture.text: Paul recalls Elijah's complaint and God's answer at Horeb (1 Kings 19:10, 18).

culture.title: Grafting olive branches
culture.text: Farmers grafted cultivated branches onto rootstock. Roman writer Columella also describes grafting a wild olive branch into an old tree.

culture.title: The firstfruit
culture.text: A portion of the first dough was offered to God, and so the whole lump was holy (Numbers 15:20–21).

Romans 12.audience: Paul turns to how believers should live, writing "I beseech you therefore, brethren" (Romans 12:1).

culture.title: A living sacrifice
culture.text: Animal sacrifice was part of both Jewish temple worship and Roman religion.

culture.title: One body, many members
culture.text: Roman writers compared the state to a body whose parts depend on each other, as in the fable told by Menenius Agrippa (Livy).

culture.title: Coals of fire
culture.text: Paul quotes Proverbs 25:21–22.

Romans 13.audience: Believers in a capital where tax collectors were openly resented would have felt the weight of Paul's instruction to pay what is owed to whom it is due.

culture.title: Bearing the sword
culture.text: The sword was a symbol of a Roman magistrate's power to punish, including by death.

culture.title: Tribute and custom
culture.text: "Tribute" was direct tax paid by subject peoples; "custom" was a tax on goods. The historian Tacitus records complaints in Rome about tax collectors around AD 58.

culture.title: Rioting and drunkenness
culture.text: Night-time banquets with heavy drinking were common in Roman social life.

Romans 14.audience: Jewish and Gentile believers who shared meals in the same homes would have heard the call to welcome one another as addressed to the very table where their differing customs met.

culture.title: Eating herbs
culture.text: Meat sold in markets often came from animals sacrificed to gods. Some Jews abroad avoided meat entirely (Daniel 1:12).

culture.title: Esteeming days
culture.text: Jewish believers kept the sabbath and feast days, which Gentile converts had not observed.

culture.title: The judgment seat
culture.text: The bema was a raised platform where a magistrate heard cases.

Romans 15.audience: Believers in Rome would have understood Paul's travel plans as a request for partnership, since Spain lay beyond any existing church's reach and he hoped Rome would help send him there.

culture.title: Illyricum
culture.text: Illyricum was the Roman province along the eastern Adriatic coast, roughly modern Croatia and Albania.

culture.title: Spain
culture.text: Spain (Hispania) was the western edge of the known world, with Roman cities but few Jewish communities.

culture.title: The collection
culture.text: Churches in Macedonia and Achaia gave money for the poor believers in Jerusalem (1 Corinthians 16:1–4; 2 Corinthians 8–9).

Romans 16.audience: Paul greets about twenty-six people by name, including Priscilla and Aquila, and commends Phebe, who probably carried the letter (Romans 16:1–3).

culture.title: Phebe of Cenchrea
culture.text: Cenchrea was the eastern port of Corinth. Letters were carried by trusted travelers, who could also explain them.

culture.title: House churches
culture.text: Believers met in private homes; Rome probably had several such groups.

culture.title: Tertius and Erastus
culture.text: Tertius wrote the letter down for Paul. An inscription in Corinth names an Erastus who paved a street at his own expense as aedile.
